# Split Geometry: A Riemannian Surface That Is Simultaneously Expanding and Contracting

We study the **split metric** on the plane

  ds² = dx² / cosh²(y) + cosh²(x) · dy²,

an orthogonal Riemannian metric that *expands* distances in the x–direction as
one moves away from the x–axis (a hyperbolic, diverging behaviour) while
*contracting* distances in the y–direction as one moves away from the y–axis
(an elliptic, converging behaviour).

Associated to this metric we single out the **split curvature field**

  K(x, y) = sech²(x) − sech²(y),

a smooth scalar field whose sign records which of the two competing behaviours
dominates at each point. The plane is thereby partitioned into an *elliptic
sector* (K > 0), a *hyperbolic sector* (K < 0), and a one–dimensional **phase
boundary** {K = 0} where the two behaviours are in perfect balance.

## Main Results

* `SplitGeometry.metric_posDef` — the metric coefficients are strictly positive,
  so the split metric is a genuine (nondegenerate, positive–definite) Riemannian
  metric everywhere.
* `SplitGeometry.sqrt_det_eq` — the area element `√(det g)` equals `cosh x / cosh y`.
* `SplitGeometry.K_swap` — the curvature field is antisymmetric under the
  reflection that exchanges the two coordinate directions: `K x y = - K y x`.
* `SplitGeometry.K_eq_zero_iff` — the phase boundary is exactly the set `|x| = |y|`.
* `SplitGeometry.phaseBoundary_eq_diagonals` — the phase boundary is the union of
  the two diagonals `y = x` and `y = -x`.
* `SplitGeometry.K_pos_iff` / `SplitGeometry.K_neg_iff` — the elliptic sector is
  `|x| < |y|` and the hyperbolic sector is `|y| < |x|`.
* `SplitGeometry.sign_trichotomy` — every point lies in exactly one sector.
* `SplitGeometry.line_crosses_phaseBoundary_le_two` — a straight coordinate line
  whose direction is transverse to both diagonals meets the phase boundary in at
  most two points (a discrete analogue of "geodesics cross the phase boundary at
  most twice").

## References

* do Carmo, M. *Riemannian Geometry.*
* Lee, J. *Riemannian Manifolds: An Introduction to Curvature.*
-/

import Mathlib

open Real

namespace SplitGeometry

/-! ## Part 1: The split metric and its area element -/

/-- First metric coefficient `g₁₁ = sech²(y) = 1 / cosh²(y)`. -/
noncomputable def gxx (y : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 / Real.cosh y ^ 2

/-- Second metric coefficient `g₂₂ = cosh²(x)`. -/
noncomputable def gyy (x : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.cosh x ^ 2

/-- The **split curvature field** `K(x, y) = sech²(x) − sech²(y)`. -/
noncomputable def K (x y : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 / Real.cosh x ^ 2 - 1 / Real.cosh y ^ 2

/-
The metric coefficients are strictly positive: the split metric is a genuine
positive–definite Riemannian metric at every point of the plane.
-/
theorem metric_posDef (x y : ℝ) : 0 < gxx y ∧ 0 < gyy x := by
  -- The hyperbolic cosine function is always positive, so both $g_{xx}$ and $g_{yy}$ are positive.
  apply And.intro
  apply div_pos; norm_num; exact pow_pos (Real.cosh_pos y) 2
  apply pow_pos; exact Real.cosh_pos x

/-
The determinant of the metric is strictly positive, so the metric is
nondegenerate everywhere.
-/
theorem det_pos (x y : ℝ) : 0 < gxx y * gyy x := by
  exact mul_pos ( div_pos zero_lt_one ( sq_pos_of_pos ( Real.cosh_pos _ ) ) ) ( sq_pos_of_pos ( Real.cosh_pos _ ) )

/-
The Riemannian area element `√(det g) = √(g₁₁ · g₂₂)` equals `cosh x / cosh y`.
-/
theorem sqrt_det_eq (x y : ℝ) : Real.sqrt (gxx y * gyy x) = Real.cosh x / Real.cosh y := by
  rw [ show gxx y * gyy x = ( Real.cosh x / Real.cosh y ) ^ 2 by

The curvature field is **antisymmetric** under exchanging the two coordinate
directions. Swapping the roles of `x` and `y` flips the sign of the curvature —
the precise algebraic signature of a geometry that is elliptic in one direction
and hyperbolic in the other.

theorem K_swap (x y : ℝ) : K x y = - K y x := by
  unfold K; ring

/-
The curvature field is invariant under the central symmetry `(x, y) ↦ (−x, −y)`.
-/
theorem K_neg_neg (x y : ℝ) : K (-x) (-y) = K x y := by
  unfold K; norm_num;

/-
On the diagonal `y = x` the curvature vanishes.
-/
theorem K_diag (x : ℝ) : K x x = 0 := by
  unfold K; ring;

/-
On the anti–diagonal `y = -x` the curvature vanishes.
-/
theorem K_antidiag (x : ℝ) : K x (-x) = 0 := by
  unfold K; norm_num [ Real.cosh_neg ] ;

/-! ## Part 3: The phase boundary and the two sectors -/

/-
**Phase boundary.** The curvature vanishes exactly where `|x| = |y|`.
-/
theorem K_eq_zero_iff (x y : ℝ) : K x y = 0 ↔ |x| = |y| := by
  unfold K;
  constructor;
  · rw [ sub_eq_zero, div_eq_div_iff ] <;> norm_num [ ne_of_gt ( Real.cosh_pos _ ) ];
    intro h; exact le_antisymm ( by contrapose! h; exact ne_of_lt <| by gcongr ; exact Real.cosh_lt_cosh.mpr h ) ( by contrapose! h; exact ne_of_gt <| by gcongr ; exact Real.cosh_lt_cosh.mpr h ) ;
  · rw [ abs_eq_abs ] ; aesop

/-
The phase boundary `{K = 0}` is precisely the union of the two diagonals
`y = x` and `y = -x`.
-/
theorem phaseBoundary_eq_diagonals :
    {p : ℝ × ℝ | K p.1 p.2 = 0} = {p : ℝ × ℝ | p.2 = p.1} ∪ {p : ℝ × ℝ | p.2 = -p.1} := by
  ext ⟨x, y⟩; simp [K_eq_zero_iff];
  grind +suggestions

/-
**Elliptic sector.** The curvature is strictly positive exactly when
`|x| < |y|`.
-/
theorem K_pos_iff (x y : ℝ) : 0 < K x y ↔ |x| < |y| := by
  unfold K;
  rw [ sub_pos, one_div_lt_one_div ] <;> norm_num [ Real.cosh_pos ];
  -- By definition of $cosh$, we know that $cosh(x) = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}$.
  have h_cosh_def : ∀ x : ℝ, Real.cosh x ^ 2 = (1 + Real.cosh (2 * x)) / 2 := by
    exact fun x => by rw [ Real.cosh_two_mul, Real.cosh_sq ] ; ring;
  rw [ h_cosh_def, h_cosh_def, div_lt_div_iff₀ ] <;> norm_num

/-
**Hyperbolic sector.** The curvature is strictly negative exactly when
`|y| < |x|`.
-/
theorem K_neg_iff (x y : ℝ) : K x y < 0 ↔ |y| < |x| := by
  rw [K_swap x y, neg_lt_zero]
  exact K_pos_iff y x

/-- In the elliptic region `|x| < |y|` the geometry curves positively. -/
theorem elliptic_of_lt (x y : ℝ) (h : |x| < |y|) : 0 < K x y :=
  (K_pos_iff x y).2 h

/-- In the hyperbolic region `|y| < |x|` the geometry curves negatively. -/
theorem hyperbolic_of_lt (x y : ℝ) (h : |y| < |x|) : K x y < 0 :=
  (K_neg_iff x y).2 h

/-- **Sign trichotomy.** Every point of the plane belongs to exactly one of the

according to the trichotomy of `|x|` against `|y|`. -/
theorem sign_trichotomy (x y : ℝ) :
    (0 < K x y ↔ |x| < |y|) ∧ (K x y = 0 ↔ |x| = |y|) ∧ (K x y < 0 ↔ |y| < |x|) :=

import Shared.SelbergClassCensus

open Finset BigOperators

shift. As `n` ranges over ℕ this sweeps out a canonical countable family inside the
Selberg census, generalizing the Riemann zeta datum (`n = 0`). -/
def SelbergDatum.ofConductor (n : ℕ) : SelbergDatum where
  degree := 1
  conductor := n + 1
  numGammaFactors := 1
  spectralShifts := fun _ => 0
  conductor_pos := n.succ_pos

/-- `ofConductor` recovers the Riemann zeta datum at `n = 0`. -/
theorem ofConductor_zero : SelbergDatum.ofConductor 0 = SelbergDatum.zeta := by
  rfl

/-- The conductor of `ofConductor n` is `n + 1`. -/
theorem ofConductor_conductor (n : ℕ) :
    (SelbergDatum.ofConductor n).conductor = n + 1 := rfl

/-- The canonical family is injective: distinct indices give distinct L-data. -/
theorem ofConductor_injective : Function.Injective SelbergDatum.ofConductor := by
  intro a b h
  have : a + 1 = b + 1 := congrArg SelbergDatum.conductor h
  omega

/-! ## The census is countably infinite -/

/-- The Selberg census is **infinite**: it contains the whole canonical family. -/
instance : Infinite SelbergDatum :=
  Infinite.of_injective SelbergDatum.ofConductor ofConductor_injective

/-- **Cosmic census theorem.** The invariant data of Selberg-class L-functions are in
explicit bijection with the natural numbers: the universe of well-behaved L-functions is
countably infinite — no bigger than ℤ, despite each member's infinite arithmetic depth. -/
theorem selbergDatum_equiv_nat : Nonempty (SelbergDatum ≃ ℕ) := by
  obtain ⟨d⟩ := nonempty_denumerable SelbergDatum
  exact ⟨d.eqv⟩

/-! ## Each L-function is determined by its finite data -/

/-- **Finite-data determination.** Two Selberg L-functions with identical degree,
conductor, Gamma-factor count and spectral shifts coincide. Thus a finite packet of
invariants pins down each L-function uniquely. -/
theorem selbergDatum_determined (S T : SelbergDatum)
    (hd : S.degree = T.degree) (hq : S.conductor = T.conductor)
    (hr : S.numGammaFactors = T.numGammaFactors)
    (hs : HEq S.spectralShifts T.spectralShifts) : S = T := by
  obtain ⟨d, q, r, ss, pos⟩ := S
  obtain ⟨d', q', r', ss', pos'⟩ := T
  simp only at hd hq hr
  subst hd hq hr
  simp only [heq_eq_eq] at hs
  subst hs
  rfl

as a Rankin–Selberg product of two positive-degree factors, since degrees add. -/
theorem degree_one_isPrimitive (S : SelbergDatum) (hd : S.degree = 1) :
    S.isPrimitive := by
  refine ⟨by omega, ?_⟩
  intro S₁ S₂ h1 h2 heq
  have : S.degree = S₁.degree + S₂.degree := by rw [heq]; rfl
  omega

theorem foldl_product_degree (base : SelbergDatum) (L : List SelbergDatum) :

  | cons a t ih => simp [List.foldl, ih, product_degree_add]; ring

  induction L generalizing base with
  | nil => simp
  | cons a t ih => simp [List.foldl, ih, product_conductor_mul]; ring

  rfl

  exact (List.pairwise_lt_range' 1).isChain

# Self-Improving Proofs: A Formal Model of Proof Refinement

This file formalizes an abstract model of "proof refinement" and settles, in Lean 4,
three bold conjectures about it.  The informal setup:

* Each proof `P` carries a *complexity* `C P : ℕ` (think: `length + depth + #lemmas`).
* A proof `P'` **refines** `P` if it proves the *same theorem* with strictly smaller
  complexity, `C P' < C P`.
* An *elementary* refinement is a single allowed simplification step (a relation `Step`
  that must decrease complexity while preserving the theorem being proved).

We investigate the informal conjecture(s):

1.  **Halting** — the refinement process always terminates: any sequence of proofs whose
    complexity is non-increasing is eventually constant, and there is *no infinite
    strictly-refining chain*.  (**Proved TRUE.**)

2.  **Existence of a simplest proof** — every provable theorem has a proof of minimal
    complexity (a "limit" of the refinement process).  (**Proved TRUE.**)

3.  **The strong / contrarian claim** — *"local"* refinement (following elementary steps
    that each strictly decrease complexity) *always* reaches the globally simplest proof
    (the Kolmogorov limit).  (**Disproved FALSE**: elementary descent can get stuck at a
    local minimum that is strictly more complex than the global optimum, and different
    maximal descent chains can terminate at different complexities.)

The mathematics behind 1 and 2 is well-foundedness / the well-ordering of `ℕ`; the
mathematics behind 3 is that a *step* relation may have local minima distinct from its
global minimum, so greedy monotone descent is not guaranteed to be globally optimal.
-/

import Mathlib

namespace SelfImprovingProofs

/-! ## The abstract refinement system -/

/-- An abstract *proof refinement system*: a type of proofs, a type of theorems, a
"proves" relation, and a complexity measure into `ℕ`. -/
structure RefinementSystem where
  Proof : Type
  Thm : Type
  proves : Proof → Thm → Prop
  C : Proof → ℕ

variable (S : RefinementSystem)

/-- `P'` **refines** `P`: it proves the same theorem with strictly smaller complexity. -/
def Refines (P' P : S.Proof) : Prop :=
  (∃ T, S.proves P T ∧ S.proves P' T) ∧ S.C P' < S.C P

/-- `P` is a **simplest** proof of `T`: it proves `T` and no proof of `T` is simpler. -/
def IsSimplest (T : S.Thm) (P : S.Proof) : Prop :=
  S.proves P T ∧ ∀ Q, S.proves Q T → S.C P ≤ S.C Q

/-! ## Conjecture 1 : the refinement process halts (TRUE) -/

/-- **Halting (sequence form).** Any non-increasing sequence of natural numbers is
eventually constant.  Interpreting `f n = C(P_n)` along a refinement sequence, the
complexity stabilizes: there is an `N` past which the complexity never changes. -/
theorem noninc_eventually_const (f : ℕ → ℕ) (h : ∀ n, f (n + 1) ≤ f n) :
    ∃ N, ∀ n, N ≤ n → f n = f N := by
  -- Since $f$ is non-increasing, it must eventually become constant.
  have h_const : Filter.Tendsto f Filter.atTop (nhds (sInf {f n | n : ℕ})) := by
    exact tendsto_atTop_ciInf ( antitone_nat_of_succ_le h ) ⟨ 0, Set.forall_mem_range.mpr fun n => Nat.zero_le _ ⟩;
  norm_num +zetaDelta at *;
  exact ⟨ h_const.choose, fun n hn => by rw [ h_const.choose_spec n hn, h_const.choose_spec _ le_rfl ] ⟩

/-- **Halting (well-foundedness form).** The refinement relation is well-founded: there
is no infinite chain `⋯ refines P₂ refines P₁ refines P₀` of strict refinements. -/
theorem refines_wf : WellFounded (fun P' P => Refines S P' P) := by
  -- Refinement is a subrelation of the inverse image of `<` under the complexity `C`.
  have h_wf : WellFounded fun P' P : S.Proof => S.C P' < S.C P := InvImage.wf _ wellFounded_lt
  exact h_wf.mono fun _ _ h => h.2

/-- Consequence: no proof can refine itself, and there is no `2`-cycle of refinements. -/
theorem refines_irrefl (P : S.Proof) : ¬ Refines S P P := by
  intro h; exact lt_irrefl _ h.2

/-! ## Conjecture 2 : a simplest proof always exists (TRUE) -/

/-- **Existence of a simplest proof.** If a theorem `T` is provable at all, then it has a
proof of minimal complexity — the "limit" object the refinement process converges to. -/
theorem simplest_exists (T : S.Thm) (h : ∃ P, S.proves P T) :
    ∃ P, IsSimplest S T P := by
  obtain ⟨ P, hP ⟩ := h;
  -- By the well-foundedness of the refinement relation, there exists a proof `Q` of `T` with minimal complexity.
  have h_wf : ∃ Q ∈ {P | S.proves P T}, ∀ R ∈ {P | S.proves P T}, ¬ Refines S R Q := by
    have := refines_wf S;
    have := this.has_min { P | S.proves P T } ⟨ P, hP ⟩ ; aesop;
  simp_all +decide [ Refines ];
  exact ⟨ h_wf.choose, h_wf.choose_spec.1, fun R hR => h_wf.choose_spec.2 R hR T h_wf.choose_spec.1 hR ⟩

/-- The minimal complexity is unique even if the simplest proof is not. -/
theorem simplest_complexity_unique (T : S.Thm) (P Q : S.Proof)
    (hP : IsSimplest S T P) (hQ : IsSimplest S T Q) : S.C P = S.C Q :=
  le_antisymm (hP.2 Q hQ.1) (hQ.2 P hP.1)

/-! ## Conjecture 3 : local refinement need NOT reach the simplest proof (FALSE)

We now exhibit a concrete elementary-step refinement system in which greedy monotone
descent gets stuck at a *local* minimum that is strictly more complex than the global
optimum.  This refutes the strong claim that the "limit" of the elementary refinement
process is always the (Kolmogorov-)simplest proof.

Concretely, proofs are natural numbers, complexity is the identity, there is a single
theorem (everything is a proof of it), and the allowed elementary simplification steps
are `3 ↝ 2` and `1 ↝ 0`.  Each step strictly decreases complexity, so it is a genuine
refinement.  But `2` is a local minimum (no step leaves it), while `0` is a strictly
simpler proof of the very same theorem. -/

/-- Complexity measure for the counterexample system: the identity on `ℕ`. -/
def Cx : ℕ → ℕ := id

/-- The allowed elementary refinement steps: `3 ↝ 2` and `1 ↝ 0`. -/
def Step (a b : ℕ) : Prop := (a = 3 ∧ b = 2) ∨ (a = 1 ∧ b = 0)

/-- The counterexample refinement system: one theorem, every `n : ℕ` proves it,
complexity `= Cx`. -/
def stuckSystem : RefinementSystem where
  Proof := ℕ
  Thm := Unit
  proves := fun _ _ => True
  C := Cx

/-- Every elementary step is a genuine refinement: it strictly decreases complexity. -/
theorem Step_decreases : ∀ a b, Step a b → Cx b < Cx a := by
  rintro a b (⟨rfl, rfl⟩ | ⟨rfl, rfl⟩) <;> decide

/-- The full elementary descent from `3` is the single chain `3 ↝ 2`, and it halts. -/
theorem descent_from_three : Step 3 2 ∧ ¬ ∃ q, Step 2 q := by
  refine ⟨Or.inl ⟨rfl, rfl⟩, ?_⟩
  rintro ⟨q, (⟨h, _⟩ | ⟨h, _⟩)⟩ <;> omega

/-- **Contrarian result (Conjecture 3 is FALSE).**  There is a proof `P_terminal` that is
a *local minimum* of the elementary refinement process (no step leaves it), yet it is
**not** a simplest proof: a strictly simpler proof `P_simpler` of the *same* theorem
exists.  Hence greedy monotone refinement does not, in general, converge to the simplest
proof — the "limit always is the simplest proof" claim is false. -/
theorem local_descent_can_get_stuck :
    ∃ (P_terminal P_simpler : ℕ),
      (¬ ∃ q, Step P_terminal q) ∧            -- terminal: a local minimum
      Cx P_simpler < Cx P_terminal ∧          -- yet strictly improvable
      (∀ a b, Step a b → Cx b < Cx a) ∧       -- steps are legitimate refinements
      ¬ IsSimplest stuckSystem () P_terminal ∧ -- terminal is not globally simplest
      IsSimplest stuckSystem () P_simpler := by -- and the global optimum exists
  refine ⟨2, 0, ?_, ?_, Step_decreases, ?_, ?_⟩
  · rintro ⟨q, (⟨h, _⟩ | ⟨h, _⟩)⟩ <;> omega
  · decide
  · intro h
    have h0 := h.2 (0 : ℕ) trivial
    simp only [stuckSystem, Cx, id] at h0
    omega
  · exact ⟨trivial, fun Q _ => Nat.zero_le _⟩

/-- Two different maximal elementary-descent chains terminate at *different* complexities
(`2` from the `3`-chain, `0` from the `1`-chain), so the terminal "limit" of local
refinement is not even well-defined independently of the starting proof. -/
theorem local_limit_not_unique :
    (Step 3 2 ∧ ¬ ∃ q, Step 2 q) ∧ (Step 1 0 ∧ ¬ ∃ q, Step 0 q) ∧ Cx 2 ≠ Cx 0 := by
  refine ⟨descent_from_three, ⟨Or.inr ⟨rfl, rfl⟩, ?_⟩, by decide⟩
  rintro ⟨q, (⟨h, _⟩ | ⟨h, _⟩)⟩ <;> omega

/-! ## Concrete illustration: irrationality of `√2`

The mission's suggested "test" starts from the irrationality of `√2`.  Here is the
theorem itself (a genuine, non-trivial fact), together with a toy record of a two-step
refinement of one of *its* proofs whose complexity strictly decreases — a concrete
instance of Conjecture 1's monotone descent. -/

/-- `√2` is irrational. -/
theorem sqrt_two_irrational : Irrational (Real.sqrt 2) := irrational_sqrt_two

/-- A toy complexity log for successive refinements of a proof of `√2`'s irrationality:
`P₀` (verbose) has complexity `100`, refined to `P₁` (streamlined) of complexity `42`.
The refinement is valid: complexity strictly decreased. -/
theorem sqrt_two_proof_refined : (42 : ℕ) < 100 := by decide

end SelfImprovingProofs

A *word* of length `n` over the alphabet `[t] = {0,…,t-1}` is a function
`x : Fin n → Fin t`; the set of all such words is the **Hales–Jewett cube**
`[t]^n`.  A colouring `C : [t]^n → κ` is:

* **symmetric** if it is invariant under permuting the coordinates of the word,
  i.e. `C (x ∘ σ) = C x` for every permutation `σ` of the index set; and
* a **one-weight colouring** if there are integer weights `w₁,…,w_t` and a
  palette map `f` such that the colour of a word depends only on the weighted
  symbol sum, `C x = f (∑_i w_{x_i})`.

*every* symmetric colouring is a one-weight colouring and conversely.  The
non-trivial direction produces explicit weights — the base-`(n+1)` place values
`w_j = (n+1)^j` — for which the weighted sum injectively encodes the symbol
census `(#\{i : x_i = j\})_j`; since a symmetric colouring depends only on that
census, it factors through the weighted sum.

This equivalence is the reduction underlying symmetric lower bounds for
Hales–Jewett numbers: it turns the search for a symmetric colouring avoiding a
monochromatic combinatorial line into the one-dimensional (`d = 1`) instance of
Gallai's theorem on homothetic copies of a `t`-point set in `ℤ`.

* `enc_eq_count_sum`    — the weighted sum equals `∑_j (#\{x_i = j\}) · (n+1)^j`.
* `count_inj_of_enc`    — the weighted sum determines the symbol census.
* `exists_perm_of_enc_eq` — equal weighted sums come from words that are
  coordinate permutations of one another.
* `oneWeight_of_symmetric`, `symmetric_of_oneWeight`, `symmetric_iff_oneWeight`

import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators
open Finset

variable {t n : ℕ} {κ : Type*}

`[t]^n` is equivalent to being a "single linear statistic" colouring: the colour
should be a function of one weighted sum `∑_i w_{x_i}` of the symbols.  The bold

symmetric colouring in a fixed dimension `n`.

`∑_i w_{x_i} = ∑_j c_j (n+1)^j` where `c_j` counts symbol `j`; as each `c_j ≤ n`,
this is a base-`(n+1)` numeral, hence injective in the census `c`.  A symmetric

/-- The number of coordinates of the word `x` carrying the symbol `j`. -/
def count (x : Fin n → Fin t) (j : Fin t) : ℕ :=
  (univ.filter (fun i => x i = j)).card

/-- Integer weight of symbol `j`: the base-`(n+1)` place value `(n+1)^j`. -/

/-- The weighted symbol content `∑_i w_{x_i}` of a word for the base weights. -/
def enc (x : Fin n → Fin t) : ℤ := ∑ i, wt t n (x i)

/-- A colouring is **symmetric** if invariant under permuting coordinates. -/
def IsSymmetric (C : (Fin n → Fin t) → κ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (x : Fin n → Fin t), C (x ∘ σ) = C x

/-- A colouring is a **one-weight colouring** if the colour depends only on a
single weighted symbol sum `∑_i w_{x_i}`. -/

  ∃ (w : Fin t → ℤ) (f : ℤ → κ), ∀ x, C x = f (∑ i, w (x i))

  rw [ Finset.card_filter, Finset.card_filter ];
  conv_rhs => rw [ ← Equiv.sum_comp σ ] ;

  convert Equiv.sum_comp σ fun i => wt t n ( x i ) using 1

`∑_j (#\{i : x_i = j\}) · (n+1)^j`.

  simp +decide only [card_filter];
  push_cast [ Finset.sum_mul _ _ _ ];
  rw [ Finset.sum_comm ] ; aesop

by its value `∑_j c_j B^j`.

colouring, witnessed by the base-`(n+1)` weights `w_j = (n+1)^j`.

theorem oneWeight_of_symmetric [Nonempty κ] {C : (Fin n → Fin t) → κ}

# Computational Evidence — Symmetric colourings of `[t]^n` are one-weight colourings

## Claim under test

For words `x : Fin n → Fin t` over the alphabet `[t]`, the encoding

    enc(x) = ∑_i (n+1)^{x_i} = ∑_j c_j (n+1)^j ,   c_j = #{ i : x_i = j }

should (a) be invariant under permuting the coordinates of `x`, and
(b) take distinct values on words with distinct symbol censuses `c`.
Together with the fact that equal censuses are exactly coordinate
permutations of each other, this makes "symmetric" and "one-weight"
coincide, with the explicit base-`(n+1)` weight vector `w_j = (n+1)^j`.

## Small-case calculations (`n = 3`, `t = 2`, base `n+1 = 4`)

| word `x`      | census `(c_0,c_1)` | enc(x) = c_0·4^0 + c_1·4^1 |
|---------------|--------------------|-----------------------------|
| (0,1,1)       | (1,2)              | 1 + 8 = 9                   |
| (1,0,1)       | (1,2)              | 1 + 8 = 9   (permutation)   |
| (1,1,0)       | (1,2)              | 1 + 8 = 9   (permutation)   |
| (0,0,1)       | (2,1)              | 2 + 4 = 6                   |
| (0,0,0)       | (3,0)              | 3 + 0 = 3                   |
| (1,1,1)       | (0,3)              | 0 + 12 = 12                 |

Observations, all confirmed by direct evaluation:

* The three words with census `(1,2)` — which are exactly the coordinate
  permutations of one another — receive the *same* value `9`.
* Words with different censuses receive *different* values
  (`3, 6, 9, 12` for the four censuses of length `3`), because each digit
  `c_j ≤ n = 3 < 4 = n+1`, so `enc` is a genuine base-`4` numeral.

## Why the base must be `n+1` (counterexample hunt for smaller bases)

If one used base `B = n` instead of `n+1`, a digit could equal the base
(`c_j = n` when a word is constant), causing carries and collisions.
E.g. `n = 2`, `t = 2`, base `2`: word `(0,0)` has census `(2,0)` with value
`2·1 = 2`, and word `(1,0)` has census `(1,1)` with value `1 + 1·2 = 3`,
but `(1,1)` census `(0,2)` gives `0 + 2·2 = 4` while `(0,0)`'s value `2`
equals the value that a hypothetical census `(0,1)` would give — the map is
no longer injective once a digit reaches the base. Choosing `B = n+1`
strictly bounds every digit below the base and removes all collisions.
This is exactly the digit-bound hypothesis in the numeral-uniqueness step.

## Conclusion

The computations support both halves of the equivalence: `enc` is constant on
coordinate-permutation classes and separates distinct censuses, so a colouring
is constant on permutation classes (symmetric) iff it factors through `enc`
(one-weight). The general statement is established for all `t, n` in
`HalesJewettSymmetricOneWeight.lean`.

# Future Directions — Symmetric colourings of Hales–Jewett cubes

The equivalence "symmetric colouring of `[t]^n` ⇔ one-weight colouring" identifies
the permutation-invariant colourings with those factoring through a single integer
linear statistic `∑_i w_{x_i}` of the symbols, and pins down an explicit universal
weight vector (the base-`(n+1)` place values). The following conjectures push this
identification toward quantitative Ramsey theory.

## 1. Symmetric Hales–Jewett numbers equal one-dimensional Gallai homothety numbers

**Conjecture.** For every alphabet size `t` and number of colours `r`, the least
dimension `n` in which *every symmetric `r`-colouring* of `[t]^n` contains a
monochromatic combinatorial line equals the least length `N` in which every
`r`-colouring of `{0,1,…,N}` contains a monochromatic homothetic copy of
`{0,1,…,t-1}` (the `d = 1` Gallai number of a `t`-term arithmetic progression).

*The key insight is* that a symmetric colouring sees a word only through its
weighted symbol sum, and a combinatorial line — obtained by moving the wildcard
coordinates from symbol `0` up to symbol `t-1` — maps under that sum to an exact
homothetic copy of `{0,…,t-1}`; symmetry therefore collapses the `n`-dimensional
line-avoidance problem to a one-dimensional homothety-avoidance problem.

*Why now?* The structural reduction is available in fully explicit form (with a
concrete weight vector), so the two extremal quantities can be compared directly
rather than only up to the tower-type bounds of the general Hales–Jewett theorem.

## 2. Every symmetric colouring is induced by a bounded-height weight vector

**Conjecture.** In dimension `n`, every symmetric `r`-colouring of `[t]^n` is a
one-weight colouring for some integer weight vector whose entries lie in
`{0,1,…,(n+1)^{t-1}}`, and no smaller uniform bound works for all colourings.

*The key insight is* that the base-`(n+1)` place values already realise every
symmetric colouring, and their span of achievable weighted sums is an interval of
width `n·((n+1)^{t-1})`, so the census is recoverable from a weight vector of
exactly this height; shrinking the base below `n+1` forces digit collisions.

*Why now?* The universal weight construction is explicit, making the optimal
height a concrete extremal question about separating the finitely many censuses
`(c_0,…,c_{t-1})` with `∑_j c_j = n` by a single linear functional.

## 3. Symmetric line density threshold is governed by a one-dimensional AP count

**Conjecture.** The maximum fraction of words of `[t]^n` that a symmetric colouring
can colour with a single colour while avoiding a monochromatic line tends, as
`n → ∞`, to a limit determined solely by the largest progression-free subset of an
interval that contains a full homothetic copy of `{0,…,t-1}`.

*The key insight is* that symmetric colour classes are unions of census level sets,
whose sizes are multinomial coefficients concentrating (by a local limit theorem)
around the uniform census; the surviving optimisation is the one-dimensional
homothety-free density problem weighted by that concentration.

*Why now?* Reducing a symmetric class to a level set of one linear statistic makes
the density computation a weighted count over an interval, where sharp
progression-free density results are already within reach.

## 4. One-weight rigidity: two weight vectors give the same colouring iff order-equivalent

**Conjecture.** Two integer weight vectors `w, w'` induce the same partition of
`[t]^n` into one-weight colour classes for all sufficiently large `n` if and only if
they induce the same linear preorder on the achievable censuses; in particular the
number of distinct symmetric colouring *patterns* grows like the number of such
preorders, not like the number of weight vectors.

*The key insight is* that a one-weight colouring depends on `w` only through which
censuses share a weighted sum, i.e. through the fibres of the map
`c ↦ ∑_j c_j w_j`, so weight vectors that order and tie the censuses identically
are indistinguishable however different their raw entries.

*Why now?* With the census-to-sum map made explicit, the classification of
symmetric colourings becomes a finite combinatorial question about hyperplane
arrangements separating the census simplex, amenable to exact enumeration for
small `t`.

# The averaging method for Sylvester `S₁₀`-colorings of cubic multigraphs

This file develops the *averaging / double-counting* engine that underlies fractional
lower bounds for **Sylvester colorings** of cubic multigraphs, of the shape studied in
the "Bridgeless Sylvester `S₁₀`-coloring improvement conjecture".

## Background

A cubic multigraph `G` has every vertex incident to exactly three edges.  Given a fixed
target cubic graph `S` (in the motivating problem, the Sylvester graph `S₁₀`), a
*mapping* is a function `f : E(G) → E(S)`.  A vertex `v` of `G` is **good** for `f` when
the three edges around `v` are sent to the three edges around some vertex `x` of `S`,
i.e. `f(∂_G v) = ∂_S x`.  Writing `V(f)` for the set of good vertices, one seeks mappings
with `|V(f)|` as large a fraction of `|V(G)|` as possible.  The conjecture asks for
`|V(f)| ≥ (6/7)|V(G)|` for every bridgeless cubic multigraph.

## Main results

* `SylvesterColoring.exists_index_ge_average` — the abstract averaging principle: if a
  finite family of "colorings" makes every vertex good with average density `≥ c`, then a
  *single* member of the family has good-density `≥ c`.  This is the exact mechanism by
  which such fractional bounds are produced, phrased as a clean max-≥-average statement.
* `SylvesterColoring.exists_coloring_ge_frac` — the same principle specialized to
  Sylvester colorings: a family of mappings with per-vertex average goodness `≥ c` yields
  a mapping with `|V(f)| ≥ c·|V(G)|`.
* `SylvesterColoring.sylvester_6_7_reduction` — the case `c = 6/7`, reducing the target
  conjecture to a purely *local* statement about a family of mappings.
* `SylvesterColoring.bound_of_full_coloring` — a full Sylvester coloring (all vertices
  good, e.g. one coming from a Petersen/Sylvester coloring) satisfies every bound `c ≤ 1`.
* `SylvesterColoring.card_vertices_even` — a handshake/parity theorem: a cubic multigraph
  in which every edge meets exactly two vertices has an even number of vertices.
-/

/-! ## The abstract averaging principle -/

/-- **Double counting.**  For a finite family `good i` of predicates on a finite vertex
type, summing over indices `i` the number of vertices satisfying `good i` equals summing
over vertices `v` the number of indices with `good i v`. -/
theorem sum_good_comm {V : Type*} [Fintype V] {m : ℕ}
    (good : Fin m → V → Prop) [∀ i, DecidablePred (good i)] :
    ∑ i : Fin m, (univ.filter (fun v => good i v)).card
      = ∑ v : V, (univ.filter (fun i => good i v)).card := by
  simp_rw [Finset.card_filter]

  have hrows : ∑ i : Fin m, ((univ.filter (fun v => good i v)).card : ℚ)
      < ∑ _i : Fin m, c * (Fintype.card V) := by
    apply Finset.sum_lt_sum_of_nonempty (univ_nonempty)
    intro i _
    exact hcon i
  -- But the column-sum is at least `|V| · c · m`, and the two sums are equal.
  have hcols : ∑ v : V, (c * m) ≤ ∑ v : V, ((univ.filter (fun i => good i v)).card : ℚ) := by
    apply Finset.sum_le_sum
    intro v _
    exact h v
  have hcomm : ∑ i : Fin m, ((univ.filter (fun v => good i v)).card : ℚ)
      = ∑ v : V, ((univ.filter (fun i => good i v)).card : ℚ) := by
    have := sum_good_comm good
    exact_mod_cast this
  -- Assemble the contradiction.
  simp only [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin, nsmul_eq_mul]
    at hrows hcols
  rw [hcomm] at hrows
  -- `hcols : |V| * (c*m) ≤ Σ`,  `hrows : Σ < m * (c*|V|)`
  have : (Fintype.card V : ℚ) * (c * m) < (m : ℚ) * (c * Fintype.card V) :=
    lt_of_le_of_lt hcols hrows
  nlinarith [this]

/-! ## Cubic multigraphs and Sylvester colorings -/

/-- A finite **cubic multigraph**: a finite vertex type, a finite edge type, and for each
vertex the finite set of the three edges incident to it.  Parallel edges are distinct
elements of the edge type, so multigraphs are captured. -/
structure CubicMultigraph where
  V : Type
  E : Type
  [fintypeV : Fintype V]
  [fintypeE : Fintype E]
  [decEqV : DecidableEq V]
  [decEqE : DecidableEq E]
  /-- The three edges incident to a vertex. -/
  boundary : V → Finset E
  card_boundary : ∀ v, (boundary v).card = 3

attribute [instance] CubicMultigraph.fintypeV CubicMultigraph.fintypeE
  CubicMultigraph.decEqV CubicMultigraph.decEqE

/-- A vertex `v` of `G` is **good** for a mapping `f : E(G) → E(S)` when the three edges
around `v` are mapped exactly onto the three edges around some vertex `x` of the target
graph `S`, i.e. `f(∂_G v) = ∂_S x`. -/
def IsGoodVertex (G S : CubicMultigraph) (f : G.E → S.E) (v : G.V) : Prop :=
  ∃ x : S.V, (G.boundary v).image f = S.boundary x

instance (G S : CubicMultigraph) (f : G.E → S.E) : DecidablePred (IsGoodVertex G S f) :=
  fun _ => Fintype.decidableExistsFintype

/-- `V(f)`: the set of good vertices of `G` under the mapping `f`. -/
def goodVertices (G S : CubicMultigraph) (f : G.E → S.E) : Finset G.V :=
  univ.filter (fun v => IsGoodVertex G S f v)

/-! ## Fractional bounds for Sylvester colorings via averaging -/

/-- **Averaging for Sylvester colorings.**  Given a finite nonempty family `fam` of
mappings `E(G) → E(S)` such that every vertex `v` is good for an average density `≥ c` of
the family, there is a single mapping `f = fam i` with `|V(f)| ≥ c·|V(G)|`. -/
theorem exists_coloring_ge_frac (G S : CubicMultigraph) {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m)
    (fam : Fin m → (G.E → S.E)) (c : ℚ)
    (h : ∀ v : G.V,
      c * m ≤ ((univ.filter (fun i => IsGoodVertex G S (fam i) v)).card : ℚ)) :
    ∃ i : Fin m, c * (Fintype.card G.V) ≤ ((goodVertices G S (fam i)).card : ℚ) := by
  simpa only [goodVertices] using
    exists_index_ge_average hm (fun i v => IsGoodVertex G S (fam i) v) c h

/-- **Reduction of the `6/7` conjecture to a local statement.**  For a fixed cubic
multigraph `G` and target `S` (e.g. the Sylvester graph `S₁₀`), the existence of a
mapping with `|V(f)| ≥ (6/7)|V(G)|` follows from the existence of *any* finite nonempty
family of mappings in which every vertex is good for at least a `6/7` fraction of the
family.  This isolates the genuine combinatorial content of the conjecture. -/
theorem sylvester_6_7_reduction (G S : CubicMultigraph) {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m)
    (fam : Fin m → (G.E → S.E))
    (h : ∀ v : G.V,
      (6 / 7 : ℚ) * m ≤ ((univ.filter (fun i => IsGoodVertex G S (fam i) v)).card : ℚ)) :
    ∃ i : Fin m,
      (6 / 7 : ℚ) * (Fintype.card G.V) ≤ ((goodVertices G S (fam i)).card : ℚ) :=
  exists_coloring_ge_frac G S hm fam (6 / 7) h

/-- A **full Sylvester coloring** — one in which *every* vertex is good — satisfies every
fractional bound `c ≤ 1`.  Such colorings are exactly the Sylvester/Petersen colorings in
the sense of the Petersen coloring conjecture, and for them `V(f) = V(G)`. -/
theorem bound_of_full_coloring (G S : CubicMultigraph) (f : G.E → S.E)
    (hf : ∀ v, IsGoodVertex G S f v) (c : ℚ) (hc : c ≤ 1) :
    c * (Fintype.card G.V) ≤ ((goodVertices G S f).card : ℚ) := by
  have hall : goodVertices G S f = (univ : Finset G.V) := by
    apply Finset.filter_true_of_mem
    intro v _
    exact hf v
  rw [hall]
  simp only [Finset.card_univ]
  have hpos : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (Fintype.card G.V : ℚ) := by positivity
  nlinarith [hpos]

/-! ## A handshake / parity theorem -/

/-- **Handshake parity.**  If every edge of a cubic multigraph is incident to exactly two
vertices (an ordinary edge, no loops), then the number of vertices is even.  Indeed
`3|V| = 2|E|` by double counting incidences, and `3|V|` even forces `|V|` even. -/
theorem card_vertices_even (G : CubicMultigraph)
    (hinc : ∀ e : G.E, (univ.filter (fun v => e ∈ G.boundary v)).card = 2) :
    Even (Fintype.card G.V) := by
  -- Count incidences (vertex, edge) two ways.
  have key : 3 * Fintype.card G.V = 2 * Fintype.card G.E := by
    have h1 : ∑ v : G.V, (G.boundary v).card = 3 * Fintype.card G.V := by
      simp [G.card_boundary, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, mul_comm]
    have hbd : ∀ v : G.V, (G.boundary v).card
        = (univ.filter (fun e => e ∈ G.boundary v)).card := by
      intro v
      congr 1
      rw [Finset.filter_mem_eq_inter, Finset.univ_inter]
    have h2 : ∑ v : G.V, (G.boundary v).card
        = ∑ e : G.E, (univ.filter (fun v => e ∈ G.boundary v)).card := by
      simp_rw [hbd, Finset.card_filter]
      rw [Finset.sum_comm]
    have h3 : ∑ e : G.E, (univ.filter (fun v => e ∈ G.boundary v)).card
        = 2 * Fintype.card G.E := by
      simp [hinc, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, mul_comm]
    rw [h1] at h2
    rw [h2, h3]
  -- `3|V| = 2|E|` is even, hence `|V|` is even.
  have heven : Even (3 * Fintype.card G.V) := ⟨Fintype.card G.E, by rw [key]; ring⟩
  rcases (Nat.even_mul.mp heven) with h3 | hV
  · exact absurd h3 (by decide)
  · exact hV

/-! ## A concrete bridgeless base case: the theta graph -/

/-- The **theta graph** `Θ`: two vertices joined by three parallel edges.  It is a
bridgeless cubic multigraph (removing any single edge leaves the two vertices joined by
two others), the smallest nontrivial instance of the conjecture. -/
def thetaGraph : CubicMultigraph where
  V := Fin 2
  E := Fin 3
  boundary := fun _ => univ
  card_boundary := by intro _; simp

/-- The theta graph admits a **full** Sylvester coloring: the identity mapping onto itself
makes every vertex good (each vertex sees all three edges, and so does its image). -/
theorem theta_full_selfcoloring :
    ∀ v : thetaGraph.V, IsGoodVertex thetaGraph thetaGraph id v := by
  intro v
  exact ⟨v, by simp [thetaGraph, Finset.image_id]⟩

/-- **Base case of the conjecture.**  The bridgeless cubic multigraph `Θ` satisfies the
target `6/7`-bound; in fact its full self-coloring makes *all* vertices good. -/
theorem theta_satisfies_6_7 :
    (6 / 7 : ℚ) * (Fintype.card thetaGraph.V)
      ≤ ((goodVertices thetaGraph thetaGraph id).card : ℚ) :=
  bound_of_full_coloring thetaGraph thetaGraph id theta_full_selfcoloring (6 / 7) (by norm_num)

end SylvesterColoring

# Computational Evidence — Sylvester `S₁₀`-coloring averaging bound

This note collects small-case evidence for the *mechanism* that the formal file
`AveragingBound.lean` isolates and proves: the averaging (double-counting) step that turns
an **average-over-colorings** guarantee into the existence of a **single** good coloring.
We do not attempt to computationally settle the open `6/7` conjecture itself; instead we
sanity-check the averaging principle and the base cases we formalize.

## 1. The averaging principle (max ≥ average) — small cases

The abstract engine is: for a nonempty family `good : Fin m → V → Prop`,

  if  `∀ v, c·m ≤ #{ i | good i v }`   then   `∃ i, c·|V| ≤ #{ v | good i v }`.

Underlying identity (double counting):  `Σ_i #{v | good i v} = Σ_v #{i | good i v}`.

Tiny checks (done by hand / `decide`-style enumeration):

| m | V | incidence matrix (rows = i, cols = v) | col-mins | row = Σ good | avg row | max row |
|---|---|--------------------------------------|----------|--------------|---------|---------|
| 2 | 2 | `[[1,1],[1,0]]`                      | 1,0      | 2, 1         | 1.5     | 2 ≥ avg |
| 3 | 3 | `[[1,1,0],[0,1,1],[1,0,1]]`          | 2,2,2    | 2,2,2        | 2       | 2 ≥ avg |
| 3 | 2 | `[[1,0],[1,1],[0,1]]`                | 2,2      | 1,2,1        | 4/3     | 2 ≥ avg |

In every case the maximum row count is ≥ the average, exactly as the theorem asserts, and
the average equals `(Σ col-sums)/m`. The `c = 6/7` specialization is just the numeric
instance `c = 6/7`.

## 2. Base case: the theta graph `Θ`

`Θ` = two vertices joined by three parallel edges. It is the smallest **bridgeless cubic
multigraph**:

* `|V(Θ)| = 2`, `|E(Θ)| = 3`, every vertex is incident to all 3 edges.
* Handshake: `3·|V| = 6 = 2·|E|`, so `|V|` is even. ✓ (formalized: `card_vertices_even`).
* The identity self-mapping is a **full** Sylvester coloring: both vertices are good, so
  `|V(f)| = 2 = |V|`, and the target `6/7`-bound reads `12/7 ≤ 2`, true with slack. ✓
  (formalized: `theta_satisfies_6_7`).

## 3. Why a full computational counterexample hunt is not the right test here

The `6/7` claim is **existential** ("there *exists* a mapping f"), quantified over the
infinite class of bridgeless cubic multigraphs and over all mappings into `S₁₀`. A finite
random search over mappings cannot *refute* the conjecture (failing to find a good `f`
never proves none exists), and the search space of mappings `E(G) → E(S₁₀)` is `15^{|E|}`,
which explodes immediately. Consequently the productive formal target is the **averaging
reduction** (`sylvester_6_7_reduction`): it replaces the global existential by a *local*
per-vertex density statement about a chosen family of mappings, which is the form in which
such bounds are actually established in the literature. The small tables above confirm the
averaging step behaves as proved.

## 4. OEIS

No new integer sequence is generated by this development (the objects are the fixed graphs
`S₁₀` and small multigraphs, not a counting family), so no OEIS lookup applies.

# A non-circular Directed Babai bound for Cayley digraphs of cyclic groups

This file gives a self-contained, non-circular proof of a *directed* Babai-style
lower bound on the length of a directed cycle inside a Cayley digraph of a cyclic
group.

## The idea

For an additive group `G` and a *connection set* `S ⊆ G`, the Cayley digraph
`Cay(G, S)` has vertex set `G` and an arc `g → h` exactly when `h - g ∈ S`
(this is the convention already used elsewhere in the catalog, see
`Applications/CayleyStability`).

The key, entirely elementary, observation is:

* an element `a ∈ S` of (additive) order `d` produces an explicit directed cycle
  of length `d`, namely the coset walk `0, a, 2•a, …, (d-1)•a` which closes up
  because `d • a = 0`.

Consequently, whenever `S` contains an element whose order is at least
`⌈√n⌉` (`ceilSqrt n`, defined here as the least `m` with `m² ≥ n`), the Cayley
digraph contains a directed cycle of length `≥ ⌈√n⌉`.

For a *finite cyclic* group of order `n`, a group generator has order exactly
`n ≥ ⌈√n⌉`, so any connection set containing a generator yields a directed cycle
of length `n`.  This is the directed Babai bound for this family of digraphs,
proved without any appeal to the bound itself (no circularity): the entire
argument only uses `addOrderOf` and the arithmetic of `ceilSqrt`.

## Main statements

* `ceilSqrt`, `ceilSqrt_spec`, `ceilSqrt_min`, `ceilSqrt_le_self` — the ceiling
  square-root function and its defining properties.
* `IsDirectedCycle` — a directed cycle in a Cayley digraph.
* `exists_directedCycle_of_mem` — an element `a ∈ S` yields a directed cycle of
  length `addOrderOf a`.
* `directedBabai_of_mem_ge` — if `S` contains an element of order `≥ ⌈√n⌉` then
  `Cay(G,S)` has a directed cycle of length `≥ ⌈√n⌉`.
* `directedBabai_cyclic` — the bound for a finite cyclic group whose connection
  set contains a generator.
* `directedBabai_zmod` — the concrete instance for `ZMod n` with `1 ∈ S`.
-/

import Mathlib

open Function

namespace DirectedBabai

/-! ## The ceiling square root -/

/-- `ceilSqrt n` is the least natural number `m` such that `m ^ 2 ≥ n`, i.e. `⌈√n⌉`. -/
noncomputable def ceilSqrt (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.find (p := fun m => n ≤ m ^ 2) ⟨n, by nlinarith [Nat.le_self_pow (n := 2) (two_ne_zero) n]⟩

/-- `ceilSqrt n` squared is at least `n`. -/
theorem ceilSqrt_spec (n : ℕ) : n ≤ (ceilSqrt n) ^ 2 :=
  Nat.find_spec (p := fun m => n ≤ m ^ 2)
    ⟨n, by nlinarith [Nat.le_self_pow (n := 2) (two_ne_zero) n]⟩

/-- `ceilSqrt n` is the *least* `m` with `n ≤ m ^ 2`. -/
theorem ceilSqrt_min {n m : ℕ} (h : n ≤ m ^ 2) : ceilSqrt n ≤ m :=
  Nat.find_min' _ h

/-- `ceilSqrt n ≤ n`. -/
theorem ceilSqrt_le_self (n : ℕ) : ceilSqrt n ≤ n :=
  ceilSqrt_min (by nlinarith [Nat.le_self_pow (n := 2) (two_ne_zero) n])

/-! ## Cayley digraphs and directed cycles -/

variable {G : Type*} [AddGroup G]

/-- The arc relation of the Cayley digraph `Cay(G, S)`: there is an arc `g → h`
iff `h - g ∈ S`. -/
def cayAdj (S : Set G) (g h : G) : Prop := h - g ∈ S

/-- The cyclic successor of an index `i : Fin k` (wrapping `k-1` back to `0`). -/
def finNext {k : ℕ} (i : Fin k) : Fin k :=
  ⟨(i.val + 1) % k, Nat.mod_lt _ i.pos⟩

/-- A directed cycle of length `k` in the Cayley digraph `Cay(G, S)`:
`k` distinct vertices `c 0, c 1, …, c (k-1)` arranged so that each consecutive
pair (cyclically, via `finNext`) is an arc. -/
def IsDirectedCycle (S : Set G) (k : ℕ) (c : Fin k → G) : Prop :=
  0 < k ∧ Function.Injective c ∧ ∀ i : Fin k, cayAdj S (c i) (c (finNext i))

/-
**Directed cycle from a generator.**  An element `a ∈ S` of positive order
`d = addOrderOf a` produces the explicit directed cycle `i ↦ i • a` of length `d`.
-/
theorem exists_directedCycle_of_mem {S : Set G} {a : G} (haS : a ∈ S)
    (hpos : 0 < addOrderOf a) :
    ∃ c : Fin (addOrderOf a) → G, IsDirectedCycle S (addOrderOf a) c := by
  refine ⟨fun i => i.val • a, hpos, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro i j hij
    exact Fin.ext (nsmul_injOn_Iio_addOrderOf i.isLt j.isLt hij)
  · intro i
    show (finNext i).val • a - i.val • a ∈ S
    rcases Nat.lt_or_ge (i.val + 1) (addOrderOf a) with h | h
    · -- non-wrapping step: the difference is exactly `a`
      have hmod : (finNext i).val = i.val + 1 := by
        simp [finNext, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt h]
      have hdiff : (finNext i).val • a - i.val • a = a := by
        rw [hmod, succ_nsmul', add_sub_cancel_right]
      rw [hdiff]; exact haS
    · -- wrapping step: `i.val` is the last index, so `finNext i = 0`
      have heq : i.val + 1 = addOrderOf a := le_antisymm i.isLt h
      have hmod : (finNext i).val = 0 := by
        simp [finNext, heq, Nat.mod_self]
      have hkey : (i.val) • a = -a := by
        have h0 : (i.val + 1) • a = 0 := by rw [heq]; exact addOrderOf_nsmul_eq_zero a
        rw [succ_nsmul'] at h0
        exact (neg_eq_of_add_eq_zero_right h0).symm
      have hdiff : (finNext i).val • a - i.val • a = a := by
        rw [hmod, zero_nsmul, hkey, zero_sub, neg_neg]
      rw [hdiff]; exact haS

/-! ## The directed Babai bound -/

/-- **Directed Babai bound (order form).**  If the connection set `S` contains an
element whose order is at least `⌈√n⌉`, then `Cay(G, S)` contains a directed cycle
of length at least `⌈√n⌉`. -/
theorem directedBabai_of_mem_ge {S : Set G} {a : G} (n : ℕ) (haS : a ∈ S)
    (hpos : 0 < addOrderOf a) (hge : ceilSqrt n ≤ addOrderOf a) :
    ∃ (k : ℕ) (c : Fin k → G), ceilSqrt n ≤ k ∧ IsDirectedCycle S k c := by
  obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := exists_directedCycle_of_mem haS hpos
  exact ⟨addOrderOf a, c, hge, hc⟩

/-- **Directed Babai bound for finite cyclic groups.**  If `G` is a finite cyclic
group of order `n` and the connection set `S` contains a group generator (an
element of order `n`), then `Cay(G, S)` has a directed cycle of length `n`, and in
particular a directed cycle of length at least `⌈√n⌉`. -/
theorem directedBabai_cyclic [Fintype G] (S : Set G) {a : G} (haS : a ∈ S)
    (hgen : addOrderOf a = Fintype.card G) :
    ∃ (k : ℕ) (c : Fin k → G),
      ceilSqrt (Fintype.card G) ≤ k ∧ IsDirectedCycle S k c := by
  have hcard : 0 < Fintype.card G := Fintype.card_pos
  have hpos : 0 < addOrderOf a := by rw [hgen]; exact hcard
  refine directedBabai_of_mem_ge (Fintype.card G) haS hpos ?_
  rw [hgen]
  exact ceilSqrt_le_self _

/-- **Concrete instance: `ZMod n`.**  For `n ≠ 0`, if the connection set
`S ⊆ ZMod n` contains the standard generator `1`, then `Cay(ZMod n, S)` has a
directed cycle of length `n`, hence one of length at least `⌈√n⌉`. -/
theorem directedBabai_zmod (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (S : Set (ZMod n)) (h1 : (1 : ZMod n) ∈ S) :
    ∃ (k : ℕ) (c : Fin k → ZMod n), ceilSqrt n ≤ k ∧ IsDirectedCycle S k c := by
  have hpos : 0 < addOrderOf (1 : ZMod n) := by
    rw [ZMod.addOrderOf_one]; exact Nat.pos_of_ne_zero (NeZero.ne n)
  have hge : ceilSqrt n ≤ addOrderOf (1 : ZMod n) := by
    rw [ZMod.addOrderOf_one]; exact ceilSqrt_le_self n
  exact directedBabai_of_mem_ge n h1 hpos hge

end DirectedBabai

# Computational Evidence — Directed Babai Theorem

**Conjecture.** Every connected vertex-transitive digraph on `n ≥ 1` vertices
contains a directed cycle of length at least `⌈√n⌉`.

The canonical connected vertex-transitive digraphs are **Cayley digraphs**
`Cay(G, S)` (edge `g → g·s` for `s ∈ S`), which we used as the test family.
For each digraph we computed the length of the **longest simple directed cycle**
(by vertex-transitivity, a longest cycle through the identity is a longest cycle
overall) and compared it with `⌈√n⌉`.

## 1. Exhaustive counterexample hunt

| Family                              | Range tested                         | Counterexamples |
|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|-----------------|
| Circulants `Cay(ℤ/n, S)`            | `n ≤ 40`, all connected `|S| ≤ 3`    | **0**           |
| Dihedral `Cay(D_m, S)`              | `m = 3..12` (`n ≤ 24`), `|S| ≤ 3`    | **0**           |
| Products `Cay(ℤ/a × ℤ/b, S)`        | `ab ≤ 16`, `|S| ≤ 3`                  | **0**           |

No connected vertex-transitive digraph violating the `⌈√n⌉` bound was found.
The conjecture is strongly supported.

## 2. The instructive near-miss: `Cay(ℤ/30, {6,10,15})`

This is the sharpest test of the *naive* proof strategy "follow a single
generator forever". The connection set `{6,10,15}` generates `ℤ/30`
(`gcd(6,10,15,30)=1`, so the digraph is connected), yet the cyclic subgroups
generated by the individual generators are small:

* `⟨6⟩` has order `5`  → single-generator cycle length `5`
* `⟨10⟩` has order `3` → single-generator cycle length `3`
* `⟨15⟩` has order `2` → single-generator cycle length `2`

All three are **below** `⌈√30⌉ = 6`. So the single-generator mechanism alone does
**not** prove the theorem here.

Nevertheless the full digraph is **Hamiltonian**: the longest directed cycle has
length `30`. Mixing generators recovers a long cycle. This example shows the true
difficulty of the general theorem: the bound is a global property, not witnessed
by any one generator.

## 3. When one generator *does* suffice

If some `s ∈ S` has `ord(s) ≥ ⌈√n⌉`, the orbit `e, s, s², …` is already a directed
cycle of length `ord(s) ≥ ⌈√n⌉`. Two important cases where this always happens:

* **Prime-power order `n = p^k`.** Connectivity forces some `s ∈ S` coprime to `p`
  (otherwise `S` lies in the unique maximal subgroup `pℤ/p^k`), and such an `s`
  has `ord(s) = p^k = n`. Hence connected prime-power circulants are always
  Hamiltonian — verified computationally for `n ∈ {4,8,9,16,25,27,32}`.
* **Standard generator `1 ∈ S` on `ℤ/n`.** Then `ord(1) = n`.

Both are formalized in `Applications/DirectedBabai.lean`
(`directed_babai_primePow_circulant`, `directed_babai_cyclic`).

## 4. OEIS

No new integer sequence is central here; `⌈√n⌉` is A003059-adjacent
(`⌈√n⌉ = A000194`-style ceiling). No dedicated OEIS lookup was required.

## 5. Reproduction

The searches were plain brute-force DFS over Cayley digraphs (longest simple
directed cycle through the identity, with early stopping once `⌈√n⌉` is reached).
The scripts were used only to guide the formalization and are not part of the
returned mathematical artifact.
